newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo inter-company debt grows to $1.4 bln.
newsitem.headline: Yugo inter-company debt grows to $1.4 bln.

text.p: Yugoslavia's internal debt grew to almost eight billion dinars ($1.409 billion) at the end of March and was seen by the Institute for Market Research (IZIT) on Wednesday as threatening to block the entire economy.

There were 22,539 insolvent companies at the end of March with total matured but unpaid liabilities growing to 7.949 billion dinars from 7.050 billion a month ago, the institute said in its monthly report.
Although the number of insolvent companies inched up 0.8 percent, their total debt rose 12.7 percent, IZIT said.
"Growing inter-company debt is threatening to block this economy unless the government urgently deals with it," an economist with the institute said.
Slobodan Milosavljevic, director of IZIT's Research Centre, welcomed the central bank's initiative to prepare a law on overall debt settlement called multilateral compensation.
"The proposed multilateral debt settlement will be good to put an end to a practice where debtors enjoy more legal protection than creditors," Milosavljevic told Reuters.

"We still do not have the draft law and cannot comment, but the good thing is that such a step would do something about debtors and creditors and help establish the rule of law in this country," he added.
The law is expected some time in May and the debt settlement should be concluded by the end of June.

Economists cautioned that internal debt threatened to slow down privatisation because it will make a reliable estimate of companies' capital impossible without identifying their debts and claims first.
The multilateral debt settlement will oblige all companies to report their debts and claims to the central bank.

"But the question is whether firms will be really motivated to abide by the law, because in some cases they have entered dubious arrangements. It's a pity that the entire action relies on their will to report true figures," Milosavljevic said.
Jovan Todorovic, head of the IZIT institute, said no revolutionary outcome should be expected from a highly technical operation.
"This operation, unknown in developed economies, serves to legalise dubious inter-company deals. But once the debt is settled, there will be a clearer picture of who really owes what," he said.
Todorovic insisted that growing internal debt was a consequence of the state's granting unprecedented protection to debtors.
Although technical, the move will be good for Yugoslavia on its way towards privatisation, he added. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
